opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to be honest about is that the competitive advantage in large models is not where a lot of people assume it is. Many people think it's the architecture, some clever trick in the network design. But if you look at the history of the last several years, architectures diffuse very quickly. A paper comes out, and within a few months everyone has it. So if your plan for building a large model rests on "we will have a better architecture," that advantage is fragile.

Where the durable advantage tends to sit is in three places. One is data, and not just the volume of data but the pipeline around it: how you curate it, filter it, caption it, generate synthetic data, and close the loop between what the model gets wrong and what data you collect next. The second is compute and the engineering capability to actually use that compute efficiently. Training at scale is a systems problem as much as a research problem. The third is the organization: a team that can run many experiments, learn from failures quickly, and keep iterating without losing direction.

So when someone asks, "Should we build our own large model?", I would turn it into a different question: "What is the thing we have that others don't, and does building a model let us compound it?" If you have unique data, for example in a specific physical domain, or you have a product that generates a feedback loop, then building a model can make sense because each iteration strengthens your position. If you don't have that, and you're essentially trying to reproduce what a few frontier labs are doing with less compute and less data, then it's very hard to justify. You'd probably be better off building on top of existing foundation models and putting your effort into the application, the data flywheel, or the domain expertise.

In my own area, which is world models and physical AI, I think the picture is a bit different from language. For language there's an enormous amount of text on the internet, and the frontier is quite crowded. For the physical world, the data is much harder to get. Video is plentiful, but data with actions, with robot interactions, with physics grounding, is scarce. That means there's still a lot of room for people to build foundation models where the advantage comes from understanding the domain deeply and building the right data engine. That's partly why we've chosen to open up a lot of our world foundation model work, because we think the ecosystem benefits when developers can start from a strong base and then post-train for their own robots, vehicles, or environments.

So my short answer is: build a large model when the model is the natural way to accumulate an advantage you already have or can uniquely create. Don't build one just because it's the fashionable thing, because the cost is very high and the advantage from the model alone erodes quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to build a large model only when it compounds a distinctive advantage, and otherwise to build on existing models and focus on applications, data flywheels, or domain expertise.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing people need to ask themselves is not "can I build a large model," but "what is the moat once I have built it." Because the honest answer right now is that the model itself is often not the moat. The architecture is public. The training recipes converge within a year or two. The talent moves between labs. So if you build a model that is roughly as good as what's already out there, you have spent hundreds of millions of dollars to arrive at parity, and parity is a terrible place to be in a commodity market.

So where does durable advantage actually come from? In my experience, it comes from three places. The first is data that other people genuinely cannot get. Not scraped internet data, which everyone has, but data that is tied to a physical process, a proprietary product, a customer base, a simulation pipeline. The second is distribution, meaning you already have a channel to the users who will consume the model's output, so every improvement goes straight into a product loop and comes back as more data. And the third is compute scale and the engineering culture to use it efficiently, which is a real advantage but one that only a handful of organizations can sustain.

If you have at least one of those three, building makes sense. If you have none of them, you should probably not be training frontier models from scratch. You should be building on top of someone else's foundation and focusing your effort on the layer where you actually have an edge.

For me personally, this is why I have become so interested in world models and physical AI. Language models are a crowded field, and the advantage there is largely about scale and distribution. But in robotics, autonomous driving, industrial simulation, the data is expensive, it is grounded in the physical world, and it is not sitting on the internet waiting to be crawled. Whoever can generate, collect, and learn from that kind of data has an advantage that compounds. That is the sort of place where I think it is still worth making the large bet.

So my short answer is: let the moat decide. Don't build because the technology is exciting. Build because you have something others can't easily replicate, and the model is the way to turn that something into a product.

r001.rationale: The response says the model itself often is not a moat and advises building on another foundation when you lack a distinct advantage, focusing instead on the layer where you have an edge.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what advantage will you have if you build this model? Training a large model is a substantial investment, and simply having one doesn’t necessarily give you a competitive advantage. You need to understand what you can do differently—whether that comes from unique data, technical expertise, or a particular application you understand very well.

If an existing model already meets your needs, building on top of it may be the better decision. But if there’s an important capability you need that existing models don’t provide, and you have a credible way to develop it, then building your own can make sense. The decision should start with the value you can create and sustain, rather than with the desire to train a bigger model.

r001.rationale: The response says to build around what you can do differently—such as unique data, expertise, or application knowledge—and to use an existing model when it meets your needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what advantage will you have if you build the model yourself? A large model takes a lot of compute, data, and engineering effort, and other models keep improving. So being competitive today doesn’t necessarily give you a lasting advantage.

If you have unique data, a particular capability you need, or a way to make the model much more efficient for your application, building one can make sense. But if an existing model already solves your problem, you should ask whether your effort would create more value elsewhere—in the product, the workflow, or the experience you deliver. Building a large model should follow from the advantage you want to create.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to build a model when one has unique data, a needed capability, or application-specific efficiency, and otherwise consider creating more value in the product, workflow, or experience. This recommends focusing on approaches aligned with one’s competitive advantage when a large model itself is not decisive.
